summary: Asked for the greatest commandment, Jesus names love for God with all one’s being and love for neighbor, and tells an agreeing scribe he is not far from the kingdom.
key_insight: Asked for one commandment, Jesus gave two and would not let them be separated: the second “is like it.” Then He told the scribe who agreed, “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” Not far is near, but it is not in. Knowing the right answer is not the same as entering.
story: When the Pharisees heard that Jesus had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together. {Mt} One of the scribes had been listening to the debate and saw that Jesus had answered well. {Mk} He was a lawyer, an expert in the Law, and he asked Jesus a question, testing Him: {Mt} “Which is the first commandment of all?” {Mk}

Jesus answered, “The first of all the commandments is: ‘Hear, O Israel, the LORD our God, the LORD is one. And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength.’ This is the first commandment.” {Mk}

“And the second, like it, is this: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no other commandment greater than these.” {Mk} “On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets.” {Mt}

The scribe said to Him, “Well said, Teacher. You have spoken the truth, for there is one God, and there is no other but He.” To love Him with all the heart, the understanding, the soul and the strength, and to love one’s neighbor as oneself, he said, “is more than all the whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.” {Mk}
When Jesus saw that he had answered wisely, He said to him, “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” After that no one dared question Him. {Mk}
differences: Matthew says a lawyer asked the question, “testing Him.” Mark says a scribe asked after seeing that Jesus had answered the Sadducees well.
Only Mark begins with “Hear, O Israel, the LORD our God, the LORD is one,” and adds “with all your strength.”
Only Matthew adds, “On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets.”
Only Mark records the scribe’s reply and Jesus’ words, “You are not far from the kingdom of God.”

fit.question: In Matthew a lawyer asks the question “testing Him.” In Mark a scribe asks because he sees Jesus has answered well, and Jesus praises his wise reply. Was the man hostile or friendly?

points.label: Same man, two titles
points.text: A “lawyer” in the Gospels was an expert in the Law of Moses, the same kind of man Mark calls a scribe. The two writers name the same person by his profession.

points.label: A test is not always a trap
points.text: Matthew’s word for “testing” can describe a hostile trap, but it can also mean putting someone to a hard test. The Pharisees had gathered after the Sadducees were silenced, and this man may have spoken for them. Mark shows how the exchange ended: the questioner was honest enough to say Jesus was right.

fit.note: Matthew tells why the question was asked; Mark tells how the man responded. One person can be both a test-giver and an honest listener.
fit.short: The lawyer was a scribe. He came to test Jesus on the Pharisees’ behalf, and Mark shows him won over by the answer.

scene.label: The Shema
scene.text: Jesus began with Deuteronomy 6:4–5, called the Shema from its first Hebrew word, “Hear.” Devout Jews recited it every morning and evening. Deuteronomy says heart, soul and strength; the Gospels’ wording adds “mind,” drawing out that the whole person is meant.

scene.label: Heavy and light commands
scene.text: Later rabbis counted 613 commandments in the Law, and teachers debated which were weightier and which lighter. Jesus Himself spoke of “the weightier matters of the law” (Matthew 23:23). The question was a real one that teachers argued over.

scene.label: Love your neighbor
scene.text: The second command comes from Leviticus 19:18, a chapter full of practical duties: leaving gleanings for the poor, paying a worker’s wages the same day, not hating a brother in one’s heart (Leviticus 19:9–17). Jesus joined commands from two different books into one answer.

scene.label: More than sacrifices
scene.text: The scribe echoed the prophets: “to obey is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:22), and “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6). He said it in the temple courts, within sight of the smoke rising from the altar.

witnesses.matthew: Presents the question as one more test from Jesus’ opponents and records the summary only he gives: on these two commandments “hang all the Law and the Prophets.” Early in His ministry Jesus said He came to fulfill the Law and the Prophets (5:17); here He names their heart.
witnesses.mark: Gives the fullest exchange: the Shema, the scribe’s warm agreement and Jesus’ verdict, “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” In a chapter of hostile questions, Mark shows one honest man among the questioners.

seeing.reveals: Jesus speaks as the Law’s true interpreter, gathering all of it into love for God and love for neighbor. He also sees the scribe’s heart exactly: near the kingdom, not yet inside.
seeing.living: Jesus did not lower the bar; He raised it to the whole heart, soul, mind and strength. No one keeps these two commands perfectly, which is why the scribe needed more than the right answer. He needed the King standing in front of him. Let these commands show you how far you fall short, and then come to Jesus, not just near Him.
seeing.ponder: Are you near the kingdom, agreeing with every right answer, but still standing outside?

preaching.big_idea: God asks for all our love, and agreeing with Jesus is not the same as entering His kingdom.
outline: A question about what matters most (28)
Near the kingdom, but not yet in (32–34)
preaching.watch_for: The scribe repeats Jesus’ words almost exactly, but says “understanding” where Jesus said “mind,” and adds that such love is more than all the burnt offerings (v. 33). He says this standing in the temple, the place of sacrifice.
